messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: Writebook lets an editor drop images straight into a page's markdown body:
each image is uploaded once and then referenced inline from the page's
content. Delete that page, and the image never actually leaves the app — the
file survives on disk, and the record that tracks it survives in the
database, forever, even once any background work the deletion sets off has
finished running. We cleared out a batch of stale pages and the storage bill
barely moved.

Fix it so that after a page whose markdown has an embedded image is destroyed,
and once any background work that destruction triggers has run to completion,
neither the image's file nor the record tracking it exists anywhere in the app.

Uploading a new image into a page's markdown, and then fetching that image back
from the URL the app hands you for it, has to keep working exactly as it does
today.

module ActionText
  module HasMarkdown
    extend ActiveSupport::Concern

    class_methods do
      def has_markdown(name, strict_loading: strict_loading_by_default)
        class_eval <<-CODE, __FILE__, __LINE__ + 1
          def #{name}
            markdown_#{name} || build_markdown_#{name}
          end

          def #{name}?
            markdown_#{name}.present?
          end

          def #{name}=(content)
            self.#{name}.content = content
          end
        CODE

class ActionText::Markdown::UploadsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: :show

  before_action do
    ActiveStorage::Current.url_options = { protocol: request.protocol, host: request.host, port: request.port }
  end

  def create
    @record = GlobalID::Locator.locate_signed params[:record_gid]

    @markdown = @record.safe_markdown_attribute params[:attribute_name]
    @markdown.uploads.attach [ params[:file] ]
    @markdown.save!

    @upload = @markdown.uploads.attachments.last

    render :create, status: :created, formats: :json
  end

  def show
    @attachment = ActiveStorage::Attachment.find_by! slug: "#{params[:slug]}.#{params[:format]}"
    expires_in 1.year, public: true
    redirect_to @attachment.url
  end
end

==================== app/models/leaf/editable.rb ====================
module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

      def has_many_attached(name, dependent: :purge_later, service: nil, strict_loading: false, analyze: nil)

        generated_association_methods.class_eval <<-CODE, __FILE__, __LINE__ + 1

            @active_storage_attached ||= {}
            @active_storage_attached[:#{name}] ||= ActiveStorage::Attached::Many.new("#{name}", self)
          end

          def #{name}=(attachables)
            attachables = Array(attachables).compact_blank
            pending_uploads = attachment_changes["#{name}"].try(:pending_uploads)

            attachment_changes["#{name}"] = if attachables.none?
              ActiveStorage::Attached::Changes::DeleteMany.new("#{name}", self)
            else
              ActiveStorage::Attached::Changes::CreateMany.new("#{name}", self, attachables, pending_uploads: pending_uploads)

require "active_support/core_ext/module/delegation"

# = Active Storage \Attachment
#
# Attachments associate records with blobs. Usually that's a one record-many blobs relationship,
# but it is possible to associate many different records with the same blob. A foreign-key constraint
# on the attachments table prevents blobs from being purged if they’re still attached to any records.
#
# Attachments also have access to all methods from ActiveStorage::Blob.
#
# If you wish to preload attachments or blobs, you can use these scopes:
#
#   # preloads attachments, their corresponding blobs, and variant records (if using `ActiveStorage.track_variants`)

I found two very suspicious things in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`:
1. `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy` — in Rails ActiveStorage, `dependent:` defaults to `:purge_later` and `ActiveStorage::Attachment#purge_dependent_blob_later` explicitly checks `if dependent == :purge_later`. Passing `dependent: :destroy` prevents the blob from ever being purged!
2. `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` is only included inside `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`, which means if `ActiveStorage::Attachment` hasn't been loaded yet in a process when `Page#destroy` runs, `ActionText::Markdown` might not even have the `uploads_attachments` association defined!

Let's test both of these right now in `rails runner` (without modifying anything yet).

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing the Image Upload & Page Destruction Behavior**

Okay, so I need to make sure that when a page with an embedded image is destroyed, both the image file and its database record are removed. I've broken this down into all possible paths for destruction.

The current system has the following behavior.  When an image is dropped into the markdown editor, it's uploaded to ActiveStorage, creating both an `ActiveStorage::Blob` (the file) and an `ActiveStorage::Attachment` (linking the blob to the `ActionText::Markdown` record on a page). This all works as expected.  When a page is destroyed, I need the linked image data to be properly purged.

My initial assumption was that the `dependent: :destroy` option on `has_many_attached` would take care of this, which would trigger the purge job to remove the images from disk. Unfortunately, it turns out that isn't what happens with `ActiveText::Markdown` as the underlying ActiveStorage code calls `purge_later` on the wrong `dependent` value. So no `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` gets enqueued.

I've also discovered a potential bug where the destroy process might not even be initiated, if the necessary `ActiveStorage::Attachment` code hasn't been loaded. This means that if you haven't touched the attachments, and then attempt to delete the page, the attachments, blobs, and even records might survive the deletion.  This also happens in environments when eager loading is disabled.

Then there is the issue of orphaned content when pages are edited. When you edit a page, a new revision is created with a new copy of the markdown content. The old page and its attachment record are *not* deleted. If you delete the leaf record, it will delete the associated `edit`, but the old, now unused page and the associated `ActionText::Markdown` is left orphaned. So if that old `ActionText::Markdown` record has attachments, those are left on disk.

So, I need to thoroughly trace all possible destruction paths. I've got to investigate the dependencies between the models, specifically around the `Leaf`, `Book`, `Page`, `Edit`, `ActionText::Markdown`, `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, and `ActiveStorage::Blob` to make sure all records are deleted.

**A Deep Dive into ActiveStorage and Destroyed Attachments**

Alright, let's break this down. My initial observation was that `ActionText::Markdown` in Writebook was using `:destroy` for its `has_many_attached :uploads` association, which immediately sent alarm bells ringing. The goal is to ensure that when a page, or any related entity, is destroyed, the associated files in ActiveStorage are *also* purged, leaving no trace. Currently, that's not what's happening.

I started by looking at how various models handle attachments: `Book`, `Picture`, and `ActionText::RichText`.  `Picture` and `Book` use the `purge_later` approach, which is the correct one. The `ActionText::Markdown` and `:destroy` was a clear red flag and needs fixing.

First, let's walk through my thought process. There are two critical scenarios.

**Scenario 1:** Normal Destruction: I need to make sure `ActiveStorage::Attachment` records and disk files *are* deleted after destroy via `page.destroy`.

I need to make sure that the `has_many_attached` association in `ActionText::Markdown` uses `:purge_later` to trigger `blob.purge_later` via `after_destroy_commit :purge_dependent_blob_later`. Right now, it's not and the records and files live on forever.

**Scenario 2:** Destruction in a Fresh Process:
This is *critical*. Here's the kicker: If `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't loaded (e.g., in a rake task, background job, or development mode), `ActionText::Markdown` doesn't even have its `has_many_attached` association defined! So calling `Page.find(5).destroy` skips destroying the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` altogether. The Active Storage records are not loaded, the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't destroyed, the `purge_later` callback isn't called, and so the image and associated files remain forever, and this is unacceptable. I have to make sure that `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is always included, even when the model isn't *eagerly* loaded. The issue appears to be related to the order of `require` statements and the use of `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`.

**Scenario 3**:
This is where the problem becomes more complex. How is the page being destroyed?
This starts with a soft delete:
*   `LeafablesController#destroy`: `@leaf.trashed!` is a *soft* delete (not what we want). I have to be really, really clear on the *intention* of the operation.  `trashed!` is not a destroy.
*   `leaf.destroy`, called through `Book`'s association or directly, will correctly cascade the deletion *as long as* the `dependent` association is set to `:destroy`. I need to ensure this is the case. This means that *all* related data should be deleted when the parent is deleted.
*   The destruction of `Book` should cascade to all `Leafs` via `has_many :leaves, dependent: :destroy` and all leaves through their relationships.

**Scenario 4**: Edits. The edit scenario turned out to be the most subtle and complex.

The `dup_leafable_with_attachments` is creating a *new* object on a `PUT` request with new uploads and keeping the *old* attachments attached to the previous record *which still exists*! `dup_leafable_with_attachments` does *not* duplicate the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` record. Instead, it creates a new record and reattaches the *same* `Blob` to it. I need to fully understand how edits and revisions work to make sure that old versions are also cleaned up. This edit scenario creates a situation where if the original page is destroyed, there will still be the original `Page` object with the `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, referencing the `ActiveStorage::Blob` and the file. This creates dangling attachments and blobs. I have to delete the `edit` versions as well, as part of destroying the related record. The relationship is `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` needs to be `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy`, to *cascade* correctly! ==================== CONTRIBUTING.md ====================
# Contributing to Writebook

## Cutting a Release

Writebook is distributed two ways: as a container image on GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), and through the legacy ONCE installer. Both need to be updated when cutting a release.

### Current Process (GHCR)

Releases are driven by **annotated git tags**. When you push a tag matching `v*`, the `publish-image.yml` GitHub Actions workflow runs automatically. It builds multi-architecture Docker images (amd64 and arm64), publishes them to `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook`, and signs them with [Cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/) using keyless OIDC — no signing keys to manage.

The workflow produces several image tags from a single version push. For example, pushing `v1.2.3` creates:

- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:v1.2.3` — the exact version
- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:1.2.3` — semver without prefix
- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:1.2` — minor floating tag
- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:1` — major floating tag
- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:latest`
- `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook:sha-<short>` — the git commit SHA

#### Steps

1. **Merge your PR to `main`.** All changes should be on `main` before tagging.

2. **Create an annotated tag.** The tag message becomes the release notes. Prior releases use terse bullet points:

   ```console
   $ git tag -a v1.2.3 -m "Version 1.2.3

   - Fix issue with forwarded headers
   - Update dependencies"
   ```

   Use `git tag -l -n99` to see how previous releases were formatted.

3. **Push the tag.**

   ```console
   $ git push origin v1.2.3
   ```

4. **Verify the workflow.** Check the [Actions tab](https://github.com/basecamp/writebook/actions/workflows/publish-image.yml) to confirm the build completes. The workflow builds each architecture in parallel, then creates a multi-arch manifest and signs everything.

That's it for GHCR. No scripts to run, no Docker credentials needed locally — CI handles the build and push.

### Legacy ONCE Process

Before Writebook was open-sourced, it was distributed through [ONCE](https://once.com) — a platform for self-hosted apps sold as one-time purchases. Some customers still run these installs, which pull from `registry.once.com` instead of GHCR.

The release script was removed from the repo before open-sourcing (in commit `0ecca477`). If you need to cut a ONCE release, retrieve it from git history:

```console
$ git show 0ecca477^:bin/release > bin/release && chmod +x bin/release
```

#### `bin/release`

A Ruby script that uses [SSHKit](https://github.com/capistrano/sshkit) to orchestrate Docker commands locally. It:

1. Sets up a Docker Buildx builder (for cross-compilation) if one doesn't exist.
2. Creates an annotated git tag (same as the GHCR process) and pushes it to origin. Pass `-` as the version to skip tagging — useful if you already tagged for the GHCR release.
3. Builds a multi-arch image and pushes it to `registry.once.com/writebook`.

Usage:

```console
$ bin/release 1.2.3       # tags and builds
$ bin/release -            # builds without tagging (if you already tagged for GHCR)
```

This requires push access to `registry.once.com` and a working Docker Buildx setup with cross-platform support.

> **Note:** This legacy script doesn't yet have a permanent home in the repo. Coordinate with the team before running it.

messages.content: Let's write and run a reproduction script (executed via `rails runner` in test environment, cleaning up afterward) to observe the exact current behavior across all scenarios.
messages.thinking:
**Reproducing Edge Cases for Asset Purging**

Okay, this is exciting! I've identified several crucial scenarios to meticulously reproduce and validate the asset purging logic within the codebase. I need to ensure robust behavior across different destruction scenarios, especially those involving ActiveStorage and ActionText attachments.

I'm thinking, let's craft a comprehensive reproduction script to really put this to the test on the unmodified codebase. The plan is to execute this script within `RAILS_ENV=test` using `bin/rails runner -e test`, making sure to clean up any temporary data after each run, or better yet, leverage transactions to maintain a clean slate.

Here's the detailed testing plan:

1.  **Scenario A:** We'll start with a scenario where a `Page` has a markdown upload, where the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is pre-loaded. We'll destroy the page, and then perform enqueued jobs. We'll verify that the attachment, blob records, and corresponding service exist, as well as the enqueued jobs.
2.  **Scenario B:** Similar to A, but the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` has NOT been touched. In a second process, we destroy the page and check the same conditions. We need to make sure that even if the attachment isn't directly loaded, the logic handles it gracefully.
3.  **Scenario C:** The classic "real editor workflow" where a `Leaf` has a `Page`, and we upload an image to the leaf's page, then edit the leaf via a markdown update, and then destroy the leaf. We'll check the associated counts of `Page`, `ActionText::Markdown`, `Edit`, and ensure ActiveStorage attachments and blobs are handled correctly. Most importantly, that the actual file is deleted from the disk!
4.  **Scenario D:** Next, a `Leaf` that is *trashed* (soft-deleted), with its associated `Page`. We'll see how the system behaves when the trashed leaf is destroyed, and the enqueued jobs are processed.
5.  **Scenario E:** This tests the scenario where we do *not* have an editor workflow, but upload via `leaf.page.body.uploads.attach`.
6.  **Scenario F:** Multiple embedded images within a `Page`. We need to verify that multiple assets are correctly purged when the `Page` is destroyed.
7.  **Scenario G:** Where the *same* blob is attached to another record, and then we destroy only *this* page. We need to confirm that this is handled correctly.
8.  **Scenario H:** We have to check how `ActionText::Markdown::UploadsController#create` and `#show` are affected by all of this.

Since `after_destroy_commit` only fires after the transaction commits, we *must not* wrap our tests in a rolled-back transaction. Instead, we'll either clean up all records at the end of the test script, or we'll use a temporary test script or `bin/rails test` to guarantee a clean environment.

Time to create this reproduction script, and run the tests! Let's get started.

RAILS_ENV=test bundle exec rails runner '
include ActiveJob::TestHelper
ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter = :test

def report(label, attachment_id, blob_id, blob_key, markdown_id, page_id)
  att_exists = ActiveStorage::Attachment.exists?(attachment_id)
  blob_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.exists?(blob_id)
  file_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob_key)
  md_exists = ActionText::Markdown.exists?(markdown_id)
  page_exists = Page.exists?(page_id)
  puts "#{label}:"
  puts "  page_exists=#{page_exists} md_exists=#{md_exists} att_exists=#{att_exists} blob_exists=#{blob_exists} file_exists=#{file_exists}"
end

# Scenario A: Upload image to Page, destroy Page, perform enqueued jobs
puts "=== Scenario A: Page with upload -> page.destroy ==="
page = Page.create!(body: "Hello")
page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
page.body.save!
att = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = page.body
puts "  Before destroy: att=#{att.id} slug=#{att.slug} blob=#{blob.id} key=#{blob.key} file_exists=#{ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob.key)}"
enqueued_before = enqueued_jobs.size
perform_enqueued_jobs do
  page.destroy!
end
puts "  Enqueued jobs during destroy: #{enqueued_jobs.size - enqueued_before}, performed: #{performed_jobs.map { |j| j[\"job_class\"] }.inspect}"
report("  After page.destroy! + jobs", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, page.id)

# Clean up leaked blob if still there
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge

# Scenario C: Book -> Leaf -> Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy
puts "\n=== Scenario C: Leaf with Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy ==="
performed_jobs.clear
book = Book.create!(title: "Repro Book")
leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: ""), title: "Repro Page")
orig_page = leaf.page
orig_page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
orig_page.body.save!
att = orig_page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = orig_page.body
slug_path = att.slug_path
puts "  Uploaded to orig_page=#{orig_page.id} md=#{md.id} att=#{att.id} slug_path=#{slug_path}"
leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "![reading](#{slug_path})" }, leaf_params: { title: "Repro Page" })
leaf.reload
puts "  After leaf.edit: leaf.page=#{leaf.page.id}, edits.count=#{leaf.edits.count}, edit.leafable=#{leaf.edits.last.leafable_id}"
perform_enqueued_jobs do
  leaf.destroy!
end
puts "  Performed jobs: #{performed_jobs.map { |j| j[\"job_class\"] }.inspect}"
report("  After leaf.destroy! + jobs (orig_page)", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, orig_page.id)

# Clean up
ActiveStorage::Attachment.find_by(id: att.id)&.destroy
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge
Page.find_by(id: orig_page.id)&.destroy
book.destroy!
'

Okay, so we've got a suspected bug. The first thing I'm going to do is make sure we have a clean, repeatable reproduction. Now, before I even *think* about debugging the code, let's execute that script with `RAILS_ENV=test bundle exec rails runner /tmp/repro.rb`. Using the test environment isolates the issue and prevents any unwanted side effects, and rails runner is the right tool to execute Ruby scripts within the context of the Rails app. And importantly, let’s run the scenario B in a new process at the same time and see if we can get it to reproduce there as well! include ActiveJob::TestHelper
ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter = :test

def report(label, attachment_id, blob_id, blob_key, markdown_id, page_id)
  att_exists = ActiveStorage::Attachment.exists?(attachment_id)
  blob_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.exists?(blob_id)
  file_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob_key)
  md_exists = ActionText::Markdown.exists?(markdown_id)
  page_exists = Page.exists?(page_id)
  puts "#{label}:"
  puts "  page_exists=#{page_exists} md_exists=#{md_exists} att_exists=#{att_exists} blob_exists=#{blob_exists} file_exists=#{file_exists}"
end

# Scenario A: Upload image to Page, destroy Page, perform enqueued jobs
puts "=== Scenario A: Page with upload -> page.destroy ==="
page = Page.create!(body: "Hello")
page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
page.body.save!
att = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = page.body
puts "  Before destroy: att=#{att.id} slug=#{att.slug} blob=#{blob.id} key=#{blob.key} file_exists=#{ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob.key)}"
performed_jobs.clear
perform_enqueued_jobs do
  page.destroy!
end
puts "  Performed jobs during destroy: #{performed_jobs.map { |j| j['job_class'] }.inspect}"
report("  After page.destroy! + jobs", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, page.id)

# Clean up leaked blob if still there
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge

# Scenario C: Book -> Leaf -> Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy
puts "\n=== Scenario C: Leaf with Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy ==="
performed_jobs.clear
book = Book.create!(title: "Repro Book")
leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: ""), title: "Repro Page")
orig_page = leaf.page
orig_page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
orig_page.body.save!
att = orig_page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = orig_page.body
slug_path = att.slug_path
puts "  Uploaded to orig_page=#{orig_page.id} md=#{md.id} att=#{att.id} slug_path=#{slug_path}"
leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "![reading](#{slug_path})" }, leaf_params: { title: "Repro Page" })
leaf.reload
puts "  After leaf.edit: leaf.page=#{leaf.page.id}, edits.count=#{leaf.edits.count}, edit.leafable=#{leaf.edits.last.leafable_id}"
perform_enqueued_jobs do
  leaf.destroy!
end
puts "  Performed jobs: #{performed_jobs.map { |j| j['job_class'] }.inspect}"
report("  After leaf.destroy! + jobs (orig_page)", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, orig_page.id)

# Clean up
ActiveStorage::Attachment.find_by(id: att.id)&.destroy
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge
Page.find_by(id: orig_page.id)&.destroy
book.destroy!
EOF

messages.thinking:
Here's my take on the situation:

**Reflecting on Job Testing Strategies**

Okay, so I'm thinking about the most efficient way to handle job testing. Initially, I'd thought about just going with `ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter = :inline`. This would be the simplest, or maybe even just requiring minitest and defining an `assert` method. But, honestly, for a robust test suite, that's not quite cutting it. I want more control, deeper inspection. Using the `:test` adapter looks ideal. That way, I can directly control how jobs are enqueued and executed. This gives me the crucial ability to scrutinize *every single* enqueued job. I can inspect its arguments, the timing, everything! I can then execute them exactly as I intend. Plus, I need to make sure I'm cleaning up any leftover garbage from previous aborted runs. A clean slate is essential for reliable testing.

cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/repro.rb
ActiveStorage::Attachment # force load so uploads exists
ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter = :test
adapter = ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter

def perform_all_enqueued(adapter)
  performed = []
  until adapter.enqueued_jobs.empty?
    job_data = adapter.enqueued_jobs.shift
    performed << job_data["job_class"]
    ActiveJob::Base.execute(job_data)
  end
  performed
end

def report(label, attachment_id, blob_id, blob_key, markdown_id, page_id)
  att_exists = ActiveStorage::Attachment.exists?(attachment_id)
  blob_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.exists?(blob_id)
  file_exists = ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob_key)
  md_exists = ActionText::Markdown.exists?(markdown_id)
  page_exists = Page.exists?(page_id)
  puts "#{label}:"
  puts "  page_exists=#{page_exists} md_exists=#{md_exists} att_exists=#{att_exists} blob_exists=#{blob_exists} file_exists=#{file_exists}"
end

# Scenario A: Upload image to Page, destroy Page, perform enqueued jobs
puts "=== Scenario A: Page with upload -> page.destroy ==="
page = Page.create!(body: "Hello")
page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
page.body.save!
att = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = page.body
puts "  Before destroy: att=#{att.id} slug=#{att.slug} blob=#{blob.id} key=#{blob.key} file_exists=#{ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob.key)}"
adapter.enqueued_jobs.clear
page.destroy!
performed = perform_all_enqueued(adapter)
puts "  Performed jobs during destroy: #{performed.inspect}"
report("  After page.destroy! + jobs", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, page.id)

# Clean up leaked blob if still there
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge

# Scenario C: Book -> Leaf -> Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy
puts "\n=== Scenario C: Leaf with Page -> upload -> leaf.edit -> leaf.destroy ==="
adapter.enqueued_jobs.clear
book = Book.create!(title: "Repro Book")
leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: ""), title: "Repro Page")
orig_page = leaf.page
orig_page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
orig_page.body.save!
att = orig_page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = orig_page.body
slug_path = att.slug_path
puts "  Uploaded to orig_page=#{orig_page.id} md=#{md.id} att=#{att.id} slug_path=#{slug_path}"
leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "![reading](#{slug_path})" }, leaf_params: { title: "Repro Page" })
leaf.reload
puts "  After leaf.edit: leaf.page=#{leaf.page.id}, edits.count=#{leaf.edits.count}, edit.leafable=#{leaf.edits.last.leafable_id}"
adapter.enqueued_jobs.clear
leaf.destroy!
performed = perform_all_enqueued(adapter)
puts "  Performed jobs: #{performed.inspect}"
report("  After leaf.destroy! + jobs (orig_page)", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, orig_page.id)

# Clean up
ActiveStorage::Attachment.find_by(id: att.id)&.destroy
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge
Page.find_by(id: orig_page.id)&.destroy
book.destroy!

# Scenario D: Book -> Leaf -> Page -> upload -> leaf.trashed! -> book.destroy
puts "\n=== Scenario D: Leaf with Page -> upload -> leaf.trashed! -> book.destroy ==="
book = Book.create!(title: "Repro Book 2")
leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: "Initial"), title: "Repro Page 2")
page = leaf.page
page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "reading.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
page.body.save!
att = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
blob = att.blob
md = page.body
leaf.trashed!
puts "  After leaf.trashed!: edits=#{leaf.edits.pluck(:id, :action, :leafable_id).inspect}"
adapter.enqueued_jobs.clear
book.destroy!
performed = perform_all_enqueued(adapter)
puts "  Performed jobs: #{performed.inspect}"
report("  After book.destroy! + jobs", att.id, blob.id, blob.key, md.id, page.id)

# Clean up
ActiveStorage::Attachment.find_by(id: att.id)&.destroy
ActiveStorage::Blob.find_by(id: blob.id)&.purge
Page.find_by(id: page.id)&.destroy
EOF

**Deep Dive into `Leaf` Destruction and Data Integrity**

Alright, let's break this down meticulously. We're dealing with a critical issue surrounding how `Leaf` instances and their associated data (specifically `Edits`, `Pages`, and uploaded assets) are managed during destruction. My immediate concern is ensuring no orphaned data is left behind, particularly media files.

The initial setup, with `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` on the `Leaf` model, immediately throws a red flag.  The implication is that when a `Leaf` is destroyed, its `Edits` are simply *deleted* from the database, not destroyed through their lifecycle. This bypasses the cascading `dependent: :destroy` relationships that should clean up related `Pages`, `ActionText::Markdown` records, associated `ActiveStorage::Attachment`s and, crucially, the actual files stored on disk. This is a massive potential for data leakage. Imagine a user uploading an image, then deleting a page.  Without proper destruction, that image file remains, taking up space and possibly leading to security or privacy issues.

Switching `dependent: :delete_all` to `dependent: :destroy` is the obvious first step, but it reveals some subtle challenges, especially when a `Leaf` has been "trashed" (marked as inactive) and then destroyed. The `record_moved_to_trash` method creates a "trash" `Edit` associated with the `Leaf`. The flow is this:

1.  When a leaf is trashed and *then* destroyed, the destroy process now should trigger the cascade:
    *   `Leaf#destroy` should cause `Edit`'s `destroy_all` to be triggered on `edits`.
        *   `Edit#destroy` should destroy `leafable`.
            *   `leafable` in the case of `trash` is the current page, which should lead to
                *   `Page#destroy` causing deletion of `ActionText::Markdown` and associated assets.
        *   This should be fine with a `revision` edit, which would destroy the previous version
            *   We will have to check if the original edit, when creating, copies the previous version or not.
    *   Then the `Leaf` itself is deleted.

2.  With `Edit` set to dependent destroy, the order here is VERY important. It will run `before_destroy` which would destroy the `edits`, the `after_destroy` of `leaf`, which is set to dependent destroy on `leafable`, and a `after_destroy_commit` which will trigger the searchable content removal.

The potential for a `DelegationError` during the `after_destroy_commit` on `Leaf::Searchable` is a HUGE deal. We discovered that if the `leafable` is not loaded, calling `leafable.searchable_content` can result in nil and a DelegationError.  If the delete from the DB is done before the `after_destroy_commit`, then we can have nil being set and the crash.

The double destruction concern has also been handled when it comes to the `belongs_to` with `dependent: :destroy` on `leafable`.

Finally, we need to consider how `Edits` themselves are related to the `leafable`.  We need to make sure `Edit#destroy` only destroys `leafable` when it *should*. Specifically, when the `Edit` is a revision, and when the Leaf is permanently deleted. This is critical to avoid dangling pointers and data corruption.  It's likely that trash edits should *not* destroy the `leafable` since the `leafable` is still present.

To summarize the high-level concerns:

*   **Data Leakage:**  The primary threat is orphaned data (blobs, attachments, associated markdown) left behind after a `Leaf` is destroyed, which is caused by the delete_all being applied on the `edits`.
*   **Destruction Order:**  The destruction order is critical. `edits`, `leafable`, and `Leaf` have to be destroyed in the right order.
*   **Searchable Content:**  We need to prevent the DelegationError on the searchable component from being triggered on deletion.
*   **Edit Type & Leafable Destruction:** Make sure to handle the case with `trash` and `revision` edits with the same care.

These are all potential issues, and we need to verify all those situations with a comprehensive test suite.

**Deep Dive into Image Deletion in Writebook**

Okay, let's break this down. First, I need to understand the core problem: Writebook isn't properly cleaning up images associated with pages when those pages are deleted. The goal is to ensure that when a page with embedded images is destroyed, both the image file and its database record are also removed, *without* breaking the image upload and retrieval flow. It's a cleanup issue related to ActiveStorage and page deletion.

My initial thought is to identify all scenarios and test cases.

1.  **Test 1: Direct Page Destruction:** Directly deleting a page using `Page#destroy` after an image has been attached. I need to verify that this action *should* trigger deletion of the `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, the `ActiveStorage::Blob`, and the file on disk. The primary concern is that the current code might not be deleting the blob and file. One concern is `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy`, which destroys the attachment, but doesn't *purge* it.

2.  **Test 2: HTTP Upload and Page Destruction:** Uploading an image through the HTTP upload endpoint (`POST /uploads`), then deleting the page. I need to ensure the same cleanup occurs as in Test 1. This also uses the upload controller, so I should be wary of any oddities that may pop up there.

3.  **Test 3: HTTP Upload + HTTP Save + Leaf/Book Destruction:** This gets tricky! This involves uploading an image via HTTP, then saving the page content (e.g., using `PUT /books/:id/pages/:id` or `leaf.edit`). The critical step is destroying the *leaf* or the *book* *after* this save. The concern is with what happens when the page is edited, which creates a new page, which could lead to zombie data!

    *   This is the critical one. When saving, the system creates a new page. The old one might have lingering attachments!
        -   Specifically, what happens to the old page? Is it properly deleted?

4.  **Test 4: HTTP Upload + HTTP Save + `leaf.reload.page.destroy`:** This is the most complex one. Upload image, save via controller (PUT), then call `leaf.reload.page.destroy`. It becomes apparent that the problem isn't just about deleting the page, but also the edit history.

    *   When the UI saves the page, `leaf.edit` runs and creates a `Page` duplicate of the previous page
        *   `Page #10` and `Page #11`
        *   The relationship between the pages, edits, and `leaf` is unclear
        *   The original page's attachments might not be purged!
        *   The new page is assigned the new attachment, but what if attachments aren't properly linked?

The key here is that when the form is saved, `leaf.edit` creates an edit and assigns a new page to the `leaf`. It is critical to investigate what `PUT` does.

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing the Writebook Image Deletion Issue**

Okay, so I've zeroed in on the core of the problem. We need to ensure that when a page with embedded images (via markdown) is destroyed, *everything* goes: the image file on disk, and the record tracking it in the database. The critical detail is that this needs to happen even after background jobs have completed.

The code seems to use `ActionText::Markdown` to manage markdown content on a `Page`. The images are being uploaded, attached to `@markdown.uploads`, and referenced inline. We have a `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy` on `ActionText::Markdown`, which is the direct culprit. When the associated page is destroyed, this `dependent: :destroy` is running, but it's *not* calling `blob.purge_later` on the attachment, thus the `ActiveStorage::Blob` and the file on disk survive indefinitely! It appears we also have some issues around how `edits` are handled and how images are attached when a page is updated.

The fix, as I see it, requires changing that `dependent: :destroy` to `dependent: :purge_later` (or omitting the option, because the default is `:purge_later`) or at least verifying that `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` is queued, so the image and blob are purged asynchronously. We *must* verify that the uploading/fetching of existing images continues to work after making these changes. It seems important to note that the prompt emphasized "is destroyed" meaning we should target the synchronous portion of the lifecycle of the object, rather than `trashed!` or a delete event in the UI.

I also need to verify that `inverse_of` is working correctly on polymorphic associations in the context of the destroy callbacks. If the `attachment.record` is not cached, the destroy callback would encounter a `nil` object, and we have a major problem.

**Comprehensive Review of ActiveStorage Destruction and Related Model Relationships**

Alright, let's break this down. The initial success with `Book#destroy` highlights that `inverse_of: :record` works for polymorphic relationships, which is a great starting point. Now, we dive deep into the specific bugs we've uncovered.

**Bug 1: `dependent: :destroy` on `has_many_attached :uploads` in `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads`**

This is a critical issue. Using `dependent: :destroy` with `has_many_attached` is incorrect. The code is structured so that it disables purging because the condition `blob&.purge_later if dependent == :purge_later` always fails when `:destroy` is used. This means files aren't removed from disk, causing persistent data leaks. The fix is straightforward: use `dependent: :purge_later` (or let it default to `:purge_later`) to correctly enqueue the `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob`. Explicitly setting it to `dependent: :purge_later` matches style.

**Bug 2: Autoloading Issues with `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`**

This is a tough one. The current code's dependency on `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment` introduces a race condition. If `ActiveStorage::Attachment` isn't autoloaded when `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` is included, the `uploads` association is undefined, raising a `NoMethodError`. The suggested solutions are to include the module directly within the class or define the association directly. After a rigorous check, including in `config/initializers/extensions.rb` is the safest, most performant way to resolve. This approach ensures the association is always available, regardless of autoloading and preloading behavior across different environments. We must make it consistent, robust, and reliable.

**Bug 3: The `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` in `Leaf::Editable` and `Edit` destruction**

This is complicated and requires a very detailed analysis of model relationships, especially with the `delegated_type` association and trash edits. This is one that should be handled very carefully and tested.

Let's trace: the core problem is related to how revisions and trash edits work, specifically with the `Leafable` associations and `has_many :edits`.

Scenario: A user uploads an image, edits a page (creates a new `leafable`), and then destroys the leaf. With `dependent: :delete_all`, the old revision's resources survive, leading to orphaned blobs and files. We need to handle `trash` edits correctly to avoid prematurely deleting the active `leafable`.

The Solution: Changing `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` to `has_many :edits, dependent: :destroy` and adding a new check in `Edit#destroy_unreferenced_leafable` that only destroys the `leafable` if no other references exist. The check `unless Leaf.exists?(leafable_type: leafable_type, leafable_id: leafable_id) || Edit.exists?(leafable_type: leafable_type, leafable_id: leafable_id)` does NOT destroy an owned `leafable`. With that check, both regular edits and trash edits will destroy the correct components.

The implementation handles all of these edge cases cleanly!
1.  Destroys the old `leafable` during a `revision` edit, which destroys attachment data.
2.  Preserves the active `leafable` while a trash edit is active.
3.  Prevents a "double-destroy" on the current `leafable`.

This also correctly fixes the `DelegationError` that can be raised if the leafable is null and helps to properly manage related attachment data.

Now, we must consider all upload scenarios and ensure there are no other places where uploads are leaked.
-   When an image upload has variants, they must be purged too.
-   The upload controller must properly create the `ActionText::Markdown` if it doesn't already exist.

**Conclusion**

With all of these considerations, the best approach is:
1.  Use `dependent: :purge_later` when calling `has_many_attached`.
2.  Use the inclusion of `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` and its setup to prevent any autoloading issues.
3.  The proposed change on the `Edit` model which properly handles the deletion.
4.  Adding these fixes to existing tests, and new tests that cover these specific cases, will fully prevent the image leak and provide robust behavior.

*   **Scenario 4B**: Destroying the parent `Book` (or the book record) destroys all its `Leaves` which does exactly the same as in 4A. Again, works fine!
*   **Scenario 4C**: What if the `Page` is destroyed directly, bypassing the `Leaf`? In this case, destroying the `page` clears the `ActionText::Markdown` record, the attachments, enqueues the purge job, and deletes the blob – also a *success*.
*   **Scenario 4D**: This is the tricky one. If we have a `Leaf` and the `leaf.page` is a new page, updated via `PUT`, resulting in an edit, and then attempt to destroy the `leaf.reload.page` (which is the updated page), does the cleanup behave correctly? The answer here is no. `Leaf` and the edit of `Page` still exist in the database! Reviewing `dup_leafable_with_attachments` in `leaf/editable.rb`, and thinking about how `Picture` works, and confirming the behavior of `Page` is 100% consistent with `Picture`. If you destroy a `Page` with no edits, or one before it has been edited, the destruction clears the blob and file. When we have edits (PUT/edit), it is only by destroying the `Leaf` or the parent `Book` which then clears *both* the current page and *all* historical edits.

Then, I turned to the issue of multiple images embedded in a single `Page`. When a `Page` with multiple uploaded images is destroyed, the corresponding `markdown_body.destroy` deletes all the `uploads_attachments`. Each attachment enqueues an `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob`. As all the jobs run, each blob record and its associated file on disk is deleted. I am satisfied that this works as intended.

Finally, I considered the edge case of a shared blob. If the *same* blob is attached to two different pages, and one page is destroyed, what happens? The `page1.destroy` process deletes the `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, enqueues a `PurgeJob`, which then runs `blob.purge`. Due to a foreign key constraint, the `blob.destroy` fails, because the blob is still being referenced by the attachment on `page2`. The `blob.purge` rescues that exception (which is a very sensible approach), leaving the `blob` record and its file intact. Then, upon the destruction of `page2`, the process repeats. With all attachments gone, `blob` and its file are finally destroyed. Here's the rub:

`to_prepare` runs:
*   AFTER #244 and #248.

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Rails Initialization and Active Storage Integration**

Okay, let's break this down. I'm looking at the lifecycle of a Rails application and how Active Storage integrates, specifically concerning when to include `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads`. I see several key points in the boot process: Active Storage attachments are defined (#244, #248), followed by `run_prepare_callbacks` (#298, `config.to_prepare`), then `eager_load!` (#299), and finally the `finisher_hook` from `config.after_initialize` (#300).

My initial instinct is that `config.after_initialize` looks clean. It runs at the very end of the boot process, after Active Storage components are set up. But, wait, let's compare `config.after_initialize` to `config.to_prepare` and even `ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_storage_attachment)`.

With `config.after_initialize`, it's simple: runs once, at the end of the boot, in every environment and for every entry point. It's safe since Active Storage components are loaded before. BUT, there's a potential issue: what if something calls `ActionText::Markdown` *during* `eager_load!` before `after_initialize` is done?

Therefore, `config.to_prepare` looks more robust. It runs *before* `eager_load!` and after Active Storage setup. Crucially, including `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` inside `config.to_prepare` is idempotent. Ruby's `Module#include` is a no-op if the module's already included, so `included` only runs once. This ensures it's always included before eager loading, before `after_initialize`, and before any request, test, or task runs.

I need to double-check that `ActiveStorage::Engine` doesn't do anything in the `after_initialize` hook that I need to worry about. I'm focusing on the `has_many_attached` definition: it looks like everything within its scope, which includes conditional variant tracking, occurs at query time, not when it's defined. And it's set up early on at #21. Therefore, `config.to_prepare` covers everything. No need to touch `config/initializers/extensions.rb`. It's better to put this logic in a separate file.

The best path seems to be placing `Rails.application.config.to_prepare { ActionText::Markdown.include ActionText::Markdown::Uploads }` (or potentially `config.after_initialize`) in its own file.

Now I need to test thoroughly: `rails runner` with various configurations in different environments (`test` with and without eager loading, `development` with reloading, and `production`), and also precompiling assets. Crucially, I have to verify that the callbacks don't duplicate on reload in development.

I think I'll go with using `config.to_prepare` and confirm everything in all environments.

class ActionText::Markdown::UploadsControllerTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup do
    sign_in :kevin
  end

  test "attach a file" do
    assert_changes -> { ActiveStorage::Attachment.count }, 1 do

    assert_response :success

    # Uploads should use relative URLs, to allow for future hostname changes
    assert JSON.parse(response.body)["fileUrl"].start_with?("/")
  end

  test "view attached file" do
    markdown = pages(:welcome).body.tap(&:save!)
    markdown.uploads.attach fixture_file_upload("reading.webp", "image/webp")

    attachment = pages(:welcome).body.uploads.last

    get action_text_markdown_upload_url(slug: attachment.slug)

    assert_response :redirect
    assert_match /\/rails\/active_storage\/.*\/reading\.webp/, @response.redirect_url
  end

  test "uploaded image can be fetched from returned URL and is purged when page is destroyed" do
    post action_text_markdown_uploads_path, params: {
      record_gid: pages(:welcome).to_signed_global_id.to_s,
      attribute_name: "body",
      file: fixture_file_upload("reading.webp", "image/webp")
    }, as: :xhr

    assert_response :created

    file_url = JSON.parse(response.body)["fileUrl"]
    attachment = pages(:welcome).body.uploads.attachments.last
    blob = attachment.blob

    get file_url
    assert_response :redirect
    follow_redirect!
    assert_response :success
    assert_equal file_fixture("reading.webp").binread, response.body

    pages(:welcome).update!(body: "![reading](#{file_url})")

    perform_enqueued_jobs do
      pages(:welcome).destroy!
    end

    assert_not ActiveStorage::Attachment.exists?(attachment.id)
    assert_not ActiveStorage::Blob.exists?(blob.id)
    assert_not ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob.key)

    get file_url
    assert_response :not_found
  end

  test "uploaded image embedded via page update is purged when book is destroyed" do
    leaf = leaves(:welcome_page)

    post action_text_markdown_uploads_path, params: {
      record_gid: leaf.page.to_signed_global_id.to_s,
      attribute_name: "body",
      file: fixture_file_upload("reading.webp", "image/webp")
    }, as: :xhr

    assert_response :created

    file_url = JSON.parse(response.body)["fileUrl"]
    attachment = leaf.page.body.uploads.attachments.last
    blob = attachment.blob

    put leafable_path(leaf), params: { page: { body: "![reading](#{file_url})" } }
    assert_response :no_content

    get file_url
    assert_response :redirect
    follow_redirect!
    assert_response :success

      delete book_path(books(:handbook))
    end

    assert_response :redirect
    assert_not ActiveStorage::Attachment.exists?(attachment.id)
    assert_not ActiveStorage::Blob.exists?(blob.id)
    assert_not ActiveStorage::Blob.service.exist?(blob.key)

    get file_url
    assert_response :not_found
  end
end
